derivation: Stem: 5 draws WITH replacement, spade p=1/4, exactly 3 spades. Third ground truth = exhaustive enumeration of all 4^5 = 1024 equally-likely suit sequences: exactly 90 of them contain exactly 3 spades, so P = 90/1024 = 45/512 = 0.087890625. The closed form agrees: C(5,3)(1/4)^3(3/4)^2 = 10 * (1/64) * (9/16) = 90/1024 = 45/512. The book's 45/1024 = 0.0439453125 is exactly HALF the correct value - the key-setter cancelled the 90/1024 numerator by 2 without halving the denominator. Cross-check on the same question's family: parts (i) 1/1024, (ii) 45/512 and (iii) 243/1024 together with the two unasked terms C(5,4)(1/4)^4(3/4)=15/1024 and C(5,2)(1/4)^2(3/4)^3=270/1024 sum to exactly 1 using OUR value (1+15+90+270+405+243 = 1024); using the book's 45/1024 the distribution sums to 979/1024 < 1, which is impossible. Ours is right.
The ANSWERS block prints only (i) and (ii) for Ex 8.1 Q.4; there is no (iii) entry. Verified independently anyway: P(X=0) = (3/4)^5 = 243/1024 = 0.2373046875, which matches our answer.

Stem: 'heads in the FIRST FOUR tosses and TAIL in LAST SIX tosses'. That is one specified outcome sequence H H H H T T T T T T, not a count, so no binomial coefficient enters. Third ground truth = the sample space of 2^10 = 1024 equally-likely head/tail sequences: exactly ONE of them is HHHHTTTTTT, so P = 1/1024 = 0.0009765625. The book's 105/512 = 210/1024 = 0.205078125, and 210 = C(10,4) - i.e. the book answered P(exactly 4 heads in any order), which is a different question and ignores the positional words 'first four' and 'last six'. Note the book's own part (i) is 63/256 = 252/1024 = C(10,5)/2^10, showing it uses the counting form when the stem asks for one ('5 times'); part (ii) does not ask for a count. Ours is right; the printed key answers the wrong event.

Stem: 10 bombs, P(hit)=0.8, so P(miss)=0.2; exactly 2 miss. Independent derivation: P = C(10,2)(0.2)^2(0.8)^8 = 45 * (2/10)^2 * (8/10)^8 = 45 * (2^2 * 2^24)/10^10 = 45 * 2^26/10^10 = 3019898880/10^10 = 0.301989888 = 589824/1953125. The printed key's DENOMINATOR base is wrong: as printed, 45(2^26/2^10) = 45 * 2^16 = 2,949,120, which is not a probability at all (it exceeds 1 by six orders of magnitude). The intended denominator is plainly 10^10 (a dropped '1'), and with that correction the book's expression equals ours exactly. Ours is right; the printed key is a typographical defect that is self-refuting on its face.

Stem: 17 riders, p = 0.05, exactly one burst tyre. P(X=1) = C(17,1)(0.05)(0.95)^16 = 17 * 0.05 * (0.95)^16 = 0.85 * (0.95)^16 = 0.3741076684. The coefficient 17*0.05 is 0.85, not 0.65; the book's 0.65*(0.95)^16 = 0.2860823346. The book REFUTES ITSELF one line later: its own part (ii) key is 2.0325*(0.95)^14, and factorising the true P(X<=3) gives (0.95)^14[(0.95)^3 + 0.85(0.95)^2 + 0.34(0.95) + 0.085] = (0.95)^14 * 2.0325 - the 2.0325 is only obtainable with the 0.85 coefficient. Verified numerically: 2.0325*(0.95)^14 = 0.9911993951 = exact P(X<=3); with 0.65 the constant would have been 1.8275. Ours is right.

Stem: two or more of 17 riders have burst tyres. P(X>=2) = 1 - P(X=0) - P(X=1) = 1 - (0.95)^17 - 17(0.05)(0.95)^16 = 1 - (0.95)^16[0.95 + 0.85] = 1 - 1.8(0.95)^16 = 0.2077719964. The book's constant is 1.6 = 0.95 + 0.65, i.e. it carries forward the same wrong 0.65 coefficient as its part (i); 1 - 1.6(0.95)^16 = 0.2957973302. Exact binomial sum confirms 0.2077719964 (sum of terms r=2..17 computed directly, not by complement, gives the same value). Ours is right.

Stem: 6 lamps, P(a lamp is burnt out) = 0.3; room unusable when the number of lamps BURNING is less than four. Third ground truth = exhaustive enumeration over all 2^6 = 64 lamp states with exact Fraction weights (each burnt-out lamp weight 3/10, each burning lamp 7/10), summing the states with fewer than 4 burning: total = 25569/100000 = 0.25569 exactly. Two independent closed forms agree: with X = number burnt out ~ B(6,0.3), unusable iff 6-X < 4 iff X >= 3, P(X>=3) = 25569/100000; with B = number burning ~ B(6,0.7), unusable iff B <= 3, P(B<=3) = 25569/100000. The book's 0.2114 is not reproducible from ANY reading of this stem: a brute-force search over n = 3..14, p on a 0.001 grid and every contiguous range of r found no (n,p,range) matching 0.2114 that corresponds to this question (the only near hits are things like B(6,0.174) at r=2, unrelated to the given data). Ours is right.

Stem: 20 devices, defective rate 3%, at most one defective. P(X<=1) = (0.97)^20 + 20(0.03)(0.97)^19 = (0.97)^19[0.97 + 0.60] = 1.57(0.97)^19 = 0.8801619777. The printed coefficient 6.97 gives 6.97*(0.97)^19 = 3.9074706909, which is greater than 1 and therefore cannot be a probability - the key is self-refuting. The intended constant is 1.57 (misprinted); with it the book's expression equals ours to 16 digits. Ours is right.

Stem: AT LEAST 6 of 8 machines produce all bolts within specification, X ~ B(8, 0.998). P(X>=6) = P(X=6)+P(X=7)+P(X=8) = 0.0001106627 + 0.0157773396 + 0.9841115531 = 0.9999995553. The book prints 1 - 1.014(0.998)^7 = 0.0001111074, which is exactly P(X<=6) (verified: direct sum of r=0..6 gives 0.00011110735) - i.e. the book took the complement of its own part (ii) answer instead of ADDING the extra term P(X=6). 'At least 6' must be at least as large as the part (ii) answer 0.99989, so a value of 0.000111 is impossible on monotonicity grounds alone. Ours is right.

Stem: 40 machines, P(a machine develops a fault) = 0.003; find P(38 or more will NOT develop any faults). Success = fault-free, p = 0.997, Y ~ B(40, 0.997). P(Y>=38) = (0.997)^40 + 40(0.997)^39(0.003) + C(40,38)(0.997)^38(0.003)^2 = 0.8867605 + 0.1067315 + 0.0062626 = 0.9997545158. The book's 775.44*(0.003)^38 = 1.0475e-93, effectively zero. That value is EXACTLY the answer to the mirror-image question: for X = number that DO develop faults, X ~ B(40,0.003), P(X>=38) = (0.003)^38[C(40,38)(0.997)^2 + 40(0.997)(0.003) + (0.003)^2] = (0.003)^38[775.32702 + 0.11964 + 0.000009] = 775.446669 x (0.003)^38 = 1.0475e-93 - the printed constant 775.44 reproduces this to 5 significant figures. So the book swapped p and q, answering 'P(38 or more DO develop faults)'. Since only 0.3% of machines fail, P(38+ of 40 are fault-free) must be near 1, not near 0. Ours is right.
